title: Road Safety Governance: Supreme Court Scrutiny, Enforcement and the Safe-System Approach

CURRENT AFFAIRS 209
Road Safety Governance: Supreme Court Scrutiny, Enforcement
and the Safe-System Approach
Category
GS
Date
Quick rule
Governance / Infrastructure
GS II / GS III
12 Sep 2026
Read highlighted facts first
FAST READ - read only this box if short on time
• Recent Supreme Court proceedings linked to the Phalodi accident have kept road-safety governance under judicial
scrutiny.
• India's road-safety challenge is multi-causal: road design, vehicle safety, speed, enforcement, emergency response
and institutional accountability all matter.
• A Safe-System approach assumes human error and designs roads, vehicles and enforcement so mistakes do not
routinely become fatal.
WHY IN NEWS
• Judicial intervention can compel compliance and accountability, but sustainable reduction in fatalities requires
continuous executive capacity and engineering reform.
• The issue is useful for examining cooperative federalism because roads, policing, transport regulation, health
response and local bodies span multiple levels of government.
TOP DATA & FACTS
• The Supreme Court has been hearing proceedings connected with the Phalodi accident and road-safety concerns.
• Road safety involves the Union, States and local authorities.
• NHAI is responsible for development and management of national highways within its mandate.
• State police are central to traffic enforcement.
• Speed is a major determinant of crash severity.
• Seat belts and helmets reduce injury risk when properly used.
• Road engineering can eliminate black spots and unsafe conflict points.
• Vehicle safety standards reduce crash and injury risk.
• Post-crash trauma care influences survival outcomes.
• Golden-hour response requires coordinated ambulance and hospital systems.
• Data quality is essential for identifying high-risk corridors and interventions.
• The Safe-System approach assumes that humans will make mistakes.
• Forgiving road design aims to prevent those mistakes from causing death or serious injury.
• Judicial orders can improve compliance but cannot substitute for routine administration.
• Outcome indicators should focus on fatalities and serious injuries, not only challans or enforcement activity.

PRELIMS
• NHAI is associated with national highways.
• Road safety is not only a policing issue.
• Safe-System thinking accepts human fallibility.
• Black-spot rectification is an engineering intervention.
• Post-crash care is a pillar of road safety.
• Federal and local coordination is necessary for implementation.
QUICK REVISION
Use the 5E frame: Engineering, Enforcement, Education, Emergency care and Evaluation/data. Add Safe-System, black
spots, speed management, federal coordination and outcome-based accountability.
PROBABLE OBJECTIVE QUESTION
With reference to the above topic, consider the following statements:
1. The Safe-System approach assumes that human error can occur.
2. Road engineering and post-crash care are both relevant to road safety.
3. Road safety in India is exclusively a Union Government subject.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
(a) 2 and 3 only
(b) 1 and 2 only
(c) 1 and 3 only
(d) 1, 2 and 3
Answer: (b) 1 and 2 only
Explanation: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Road safety responsibilities are distributed across Union, State and local
institutions.

PROBABLE MAINS QUESTION
Judicial directions can catalyse road-safety reform, but cannot substitute for a Safe-System approach. Analyse the
institutional and policy measures needed to reduce road fatalities in India.
MODEL ANSWER - ~300 WORDS
INTRODUCTION
Judicial intervention can compel compliance and accountability, but sustainable reduction in fatalities requires
continuous executive capacity and engineering reform. A Safe-System approach assumes human error and designs
roads, vehicles and enforcement so mistakes do not routinely become fatal.
SIGNIFICANCE
• Safer roads reduce preventable deaths, disability and household economic loss.
• Engineering-based prevention is less dependent on perfect human behaviour.
• Reliable data allows scarce enforcement and infrastructure resources to target the highest-risk locations.
CHALLENGES
• Fragmented responsibility can weaken accountability.
• Enforcement may be episodic rather than risk-based and sustained.
• Trauma-care capacity and response times vary widely across regions.
WAY FORWARD
• Adopt corridor-level Safe-System audits and time-bound black-spot correction.
• Integrate crash, hospital, vehicle and enforcement data for evidence-based action.
• Measure agencies against fatality reduction and emergency-response outcomes, not merely activity counts.
Accountability should be outcome-based. States and road agencies can publish corridor-wise fatality trends, black-spot correction status, ambulance response times and compliance with safety audits. Such indicators help courts, legislatures and citizens distinguish temporary enforcement drives from sustained institutional improvement. Funding should follow evidence of risk so that high-fatality corridors receive engineering and trauma-care interventions first.

CONCLUSION
Courts can force attention to failures, but lasting road safety comes from institutions that continuously engineer risk out
of the transport system and learn from every serious crash.
A road-safety programme should begin with where people are dying, not with uniform enforcement targets. Corridor
crash data can identify dangerous speeds, junctions, median openings and pedestrian conflict points; engineering
changes can then be prioritised by expected fatality reduction. Automated enforcement should be transparent and
paired with safer street design. Trauma networks need mapped ambulance coverage and referral protocols so serious
injuries reach capable hospitals quickly. Independent post-crash reviews can convert each fatal incident into design and
enforcement lessons, creating a continuous prevention cycle.
